sentences.text: Cetiosaurus was a primitive, quadrupedal herbivore characterized by a long neck, a small head, and relatively long forelimbs.
The skull remains largely unknown, though a brain case may be represented by specimen OUMNH J13596, and the tail was considerably shorter than in most sauropods.
The best-known specimen, C. oxoniensis, displayed at Leicester Museum and Art Gallery, is 15 meters long and includes fourteen cervical, ten dorsal, five sacral, and about fifty caudal vertebrae.
Sir Richard Owen initially did not recognize Cetiosaurus as a dinosaur, considering it a gigantic reptile that lived in the sea with crocodilian characteristics.
Cetiosaurus holds the distinction of being the first sauropod dinosaur to be described from bones, named in 1842 by Sir Richard Owen.
Owen named the genus in 1841, one year before he coined the term Dinosauria, based on three more or less complete specimens discovered starting from 1868.
These skeletons were found near Bletchingdon in a Bathonian layer by workers and Professor John Phillips, making the genus known from three skeletons discovered by the Phillips family.

John Whitaker Hulke named Cetiosaurus humerocristatus in 1874 based on a humerus found at Sandsfoot near Weymouth in Dorset, while C. oxoniensis, named by Phillips in 1871, is the type species of the genus.
Paul considered Cetiosaurus a feeding generalist that ate at both low and medium-high levels, based on its moderately long neck and limb proportions.
Unlike most other sauropods, Cetiosaurus had forelimbs equal in length to its hindlimbs because its forearm was as long as its upper arm.
C. oxoniensis was officially designated as the type species of the genus Cetiosaurus in 2014, whereas C. brachyurus is considered a nomen dubium, and C. rigauxi is not a sauropod but a pliosaurid.
Paul Upchurch and John Martin determined in 2003 that Cetiosaurus hypoolithicus and Cetiosaurus epioolithicus were invalid because they were nomina nuda.
Cetiosaurus lived during the Middle Jurassic period, between 171 and 165 million years ago, in what is now Britain and possibly France.
Vertebrae of a related species were found in the Early Cretaceous Wessex Formation of the Isle of Wight, and C. oxoniensis is the best-known species from the Middle Jurassic.
It was determined in 1849 that some bones previously assigned to Cetiosaurus actually belonged to Iguanodontidae rather than sauropods.

It is debated whether Cetiosaurus humerocristatus is a valid taxon, as it is often considered a nomen dubium, and whether Cetiosaurus brevis should be the type species, as this would cause taxonomic instability with the genus Pelorosaurus.
It is also debated why the dinosaurs of the London-Brabant Massif did not experience insular dwarfism despite the island's size.
Fossil tracks discovered in Oxfordshire in 1997 and 2024 are suggested to be Cetiosaurus footprints, though they could also belong to a diplodocoid.
